nameStory: Field locoweed gets its intriguing name from the Spanish word 'loco,' meaning crazy, because some species in this plant family can make livestock behave erratically if eaten in large quantities. The 'field' part simply refers to its preference for open meadows and prairies rather than deep forests.
description: Field locoweed is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms compact clumps close to the ground. This hardy little plant produces clusters of small, pea-like flowers that rise above silvery-green, feathery leaves. As a member of the legume family, it's related to beans and peas, and typically grows just 6-12 inches tall. It's quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, pea-like flowers clustered in dense spikes that rise above the leaves. The flowers are typically cream, white, or pale yellow, with the characteristic irregular shape of legume flowers - like tiny sweet pea blossoms.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with many small, narrow leaflets arranged along a central stem, creating a feathery appearance. The leaves feel soft and silky to the touch, often with a silvery-green color due to fine hairs.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, cushion-like clumps that hug the ground, rarely exceeding a foot in height. The whole plant has a compact, mounded appearance that helps it withstand harsh mountain conditions.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, inflated pods that feel papery when mature. These seed pods are characteristic of the legume family and may be slightly fuzzy or smooth depending on the variety.

habitat: In New England, field locoweed is extremely rare and typically found in rocky, gravelly areas with excellent drainage, such as mountain slopes or exposed ridges. It prefers open, sunny locations with poor, alkaline soils where few other plants can thrive. Look for it in areas that experience harsh conditions - the kind of spots where mountain wildflowers and alpine plants make their home.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of silvery-green compound leaves. The plant begins to form its characteristic low mounds as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time, when the distinctive pea-like flowers appear in dense clusters above the foliage. This is the best time for identification when flowers are fresh and colorful.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and turn brown, while leaves may begin to yellow. The compact growth form becomes more apparent as other vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in harsh climates, though some basal leaves may persist in protected locations. Only the root system survives underground.

funFact: Field locoweed is a larval host plant for the small blue butterfly, meaning this tiny plant plays a crucial role in supporting one of our most delicate pollinators - the butterfly caterpillars literally cannot survive without it!
confusionNotes: Field locoweed might be confused with wild vetch or other small legumes, but its distinctive cushion-like growth habit and silvery, finely-divided leaves set it apart. Remember: locoweed stays low and compact, while vetches tend to be climbing or sprawling plants.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its somewhat alarming common name, field locoweed in New England is not considered dangerous to humans or livestock in normal circumstances. The 'loco' effects are primarily associated with western species and typically only occur when animals consume large quantities over extended periods.
compareHints: Field locoweed is the only Oxytropis species commonly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other small legumes in the region like wild vetch or clover, field locoweed has a much more compact, cushioned growth form and distinctively silvery, finely-divided foliage. Its preference for rocky, harsh conditions also sets it apart from most other regional legumes that prefer richer soils.
